What a junior PM should learn first now

If the grunt work that taught me the craft is gone, how do I learn the craft?

1. A programme due on Friday

On Monday, 12 January 2026, Meera Raghavan sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Samvit Commerce Cloud's office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru with a document open that she had written in 2022 and had not meaningfully changed since. It was the twelve-week onboarding programme for Samvit's associate product manager cohort. Five APMs — three from campus, two internal transfers from customer success — were joining on Monday, 2 February. Meera, Director of Product, had to hand the revised programme to the people team by Friday, 23 January.

The 2022 programme had a clear spine. Weeks one to three: shadow a senior PM, write release notes for every shipped item. Weeks four to seven: own the bug triage queue for one surface and write the weekly quality summary. Weeks eight to twelve: write two product requirement documents end to end, each reviewed line by line by a senior PM. It had produced four competent product managers in three years. Meera had run it twice herself.

The problem was that by January 2026, every task on that list took a fraction of the time it had taken in 2022, and none of them was any longer a task a person did alone. Release notes were drafted from merged pull requests by an internal assistant and edited in about four minutes. The bug queue was clustered and summarised automatically each Monday at 06:00. A first-draft PRD, complete with competitive scan, acceptance criteria and a serviceable metrics section, arrived twenty-five minutes after someone typed three paragraphs of intent. Samvit's own engineering leadership had built most of this.

The week before, Arvind Sreenivasan, Samvit's VP of Engineering, had put a proposal in front of the leadership group: cancel the APM cohort and convert the budget — about ₹1.1 crore a year, fully loaded — into two senior product managers. His argument was not hostile. It was that the cohort's first-year output had always been modest, and that its value had been the pipeline; if the tasks that built the pipeline no longer built anything, the pipeline was an expensive fiction. Meera did not think he was wrong about the premise. She thought he was wrong about the conclusion, and she had eleven days to say why in a document.

2. The idea

The idea Meera needed is best stated as a distinction between three different things a product manager does, which the old apprenticeship had bundled together so tightly that nobody separated them.

Production is making the artefact: the document, the analysis, the deck, the summary of thirty customer calls. Evaluation is deciding whether the artefact in front of you is any good — whether the analysis is sound, whether the requirement is the right requirement, whether the summary has lost the one sentence that mattered. Specification is deciding what artefact should exist at all: which question is worth asking this quarter.

Until about 2023, a junior product manager acquired evaluation almost entirely as a by-product of production. You wrote the thing slowly, badly, and in public; a senior corrected it; over thirty repetitions your sense of what "good" felt like drifted into calibration. Nobody designed this. It was free, because the production work had to be done by someone and juniors were the cheapest someone. The educational sociologists Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger named the general pattern in 1991: legitimate peripheral participation, in which a newcomer learns a craft by doing real but low-consequence parts of the real work at its edge.

What has changed is that the cost of production has collapsed while the cost of evaluation has not. The low-consequence edge tasks — the rungs a newcomer climbed — are the ones automation reaches first. This is not new either. Lisanne Bainbridge described it in 1983 in a short paper called "Ironies of Automation": automating the routine parts of a job removes exactly the practice that built the skill the operator needs for the non-routine parts, and leaves the human with only the hard cases and no way to have got good at them.

So the sentence Meera could say in a leadership meeting without sounding glib was this: automation took the rungs, not the ladder — what a junior needs first now is deliberate repetitions at judging work, because the repetitions at producing it no longer arrive for free.

3. How it actually works

The method Meera eventually used has four steps, and the third is the one practitioners usually leave implicit.

The first step is a task ledger. List every artefact a junior would have produced in their first twelve months, and mark each one P, E or S — production, evaluation or specification. Then, against each, write two things: how long it took a junior in 2022, and how long it takes now. The gap is not a productivity saving. It is a measure of learning that has quietly left the building.

The second step is to measure the feedback loop, not the task. The psychologist Robin Hogarth, writing in Educating Intuition in 2001, distinguished kind learning environments, where feedback is fast, accurate and unambiguous, from wicked ones, where it is slow, noisy and attributable to many causes. Chess is kind. Product management is mostly wicked: a roadmap decision taken in February pays out, if at all, in October, confounded by a pricing change and a competitor's launch. Intuition only calibrates in kind environments. So the practical question is not "what should the junior do?" but "when will this junior find out they were wrong, and how clearly?"

The third step — the implicit one — is the pre-commitment. A repetition only teaches if the learner committed to a judgement before seeing the answer. Reviewing an AI-drafted document and approving it is not a repetition; it is ratification, and it teaches nothing, because the mind that reads a confident draft cannot recover what it would have thought unaided. The fix is mechanical: the junior writes down their own answer first — the number they expect, the requirement they would cut, the option they would pick and why — and only then opens the draft. The deliverable is the difference between the two, and the argument for it.

The fourth step is allocating senior attention. In the old model, a senior PM's coaching time was spent correcting prose and analysis. That correction is now largely unnecessary: the prose is fine, the analysis is competently structured. The same hours can instead be spent on judgement — on why this requirement and not that one. Senior attention, not tooling, is the binding constraint, and the arithmetic of how it is spent determines almost everything.

4. A worked example

Meera wanted a number, because Arvind would want a number. She defined a calibrated repetition as one instance in which an APM committed to a judgement in writing and then received a specific correction from someone who knew better. Everything else — reading, shadowing, approving drafts — she counted as zero.

Under the 2022 programme, an APM produced roughly 30 substantial artefacts in the first year. Each carried one implicit commitment, and each received on average 40 minutes of senior review. That is 30 calibrated repetitions, consuming 30 × 40 ÷ 60 = 20 senior hours per APM per year.

Under the 2026 default — the same programme run with the new tooling and no other change — the APM still produced 30 artefacts, but the drafts arrived polished. Senior review dropped, by Meera's sampling of the previous cohort, to about 10 minutes each, and in perhaps a quarter of cases the APM had formed no independent view at all before reading the draft. Calibrated repetitions: roughly 30 × 0.25 = 8 per year, on 5 senior hours. The programme had lost 73 per cent of its teaching value while looking identical on paper.

Now the design. Samvit's four senior PMs could each protect 4 hours a week for coaching — 4 × 4 × 46 working weeks = 736 hours a year — but only about 200 of those were genuinely available across the five-person cohort after existing commitments, which is 40 hours per APM per year. At Meera's proposed format, a pre-committed judgement plus a 25-minute correction conversation, that buys 40 × 60 ÷ 25 = 96 calibrated repetitions per APM per year, against 30 in the old world. The cohort was not unaffordable. It was mis-specified.

Then the sensitivity pass, because one input was fragile. Suppose senior availability halves — two of the four senior PMs are pulled onto a platform migration, a thing that happens every year at Samvit. Coaching drops to 20 hours per APM, and repetitions fall to 48. Still better than 30, but the margin is thin. Meera therefore split the format: half the repetitions as 25-minute live conversations, half as written pre-commitments answered asynchronously in about 10 minutes of senior time. At 10 hours live (24 reps) and 10 hours written (60 reps), the same 20 hours buys 84 repetitions. The lesson from the second pass was not the number. It was that the cheap lever is not senior hours; it is the duration of a repetition, and that duration is set by how well the junior has pre-committed in writing.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Production fluency is routinely mistaken for evaluation skill

The most common error is to look at a junior who can generate five plausible options in ten minutes and conclude that they understand the problem. Generating and ranking are different faculties, and the first has become almost free while the second has not. The tell is simple: ask which of the five they would kill first. A junior with production fluency and no evaluation skill will hesitate, then defend all five.

"Judgement first" does not mean skipping the mechanics

You cannot evaluate a cohort analysis you could not, in principle, have produced. Threshold competence in the underlying craft remains a prerequisite — it has simply changed from a ladder you climb to a floor you must stand on. The distinction matters because the two prescriptions look opposite: one says do the drudgery, the other says skip it. The correct reading is that you must be able to do it once, carefully, and then need not do it a hundred times.

Feedback latency, not tooling, is the binding constraint

Most of what determines whether a junior learns has nothing to do with which assistant the company licenses. It is whether the environment returns a verdict within days or within quarters, and whether that verdict is attributable. A team that ships weekly to two hundred thousand users is a kinder classroom than a team that ships quarterly to nine enterprise accounts, regardless of tooling.

Volume of output is not volume of learning

An APM who ships forty documents in a year where their predecessor shipped fifteen has not learned 2.7 times as much; they may have learned less. This is Bainbridge's irony in its exact form. The diagnostic is the pre-commitment log: if no judgement was recorded before the answer appeared, the count of artefacts is a measure of throughput and nothing else.

Taste is domain-specific and transfers badly

Judgement about consumer onboarding flows does not confer judgement about insurance claims adjudication or warehouse slotting. A junior who has built calibration in one surface will over-apply it to the next, and seniors will read the resulting confidence as competence. This bounds how portable any judgement-first training is, and it argues for depth in one surface before breadth.

What the idea cannot tell you is how long it takes

There is no honest answer yet to the question "how many months until an AI-native junior is as sound as a 2019 junior at year three?" No cohort has been through an AI-era apprenticeship and come out the other end senior. Anyone offering a number is extrapolating from the old curve. A thoughtful newcomer should treat confident timelines — in either direction — as the weakest part of any argument they hear, including this one.

It is confused with AI literacy, and they are not the same

Tool fluency is now table stakes: assumed, unremarkable, and depreciating every time a model is replaced. It is not what distinguishes people. The confusion is costly because a tool curriculum is easy to write and easy to measure, and a judgement curriculum is neither, so organisations drift toward the first and report it as the second.

The organisation's incentives run against the junior's

A team that gives juniors genuine judgement repetitions ships a little slower this quarter. Under the old model that cost was hidden inside production work that had to be done anyway. Now it is a visible line item — senior hours spent not shipping — and visible costs get cut first. Before relying on any programme, a newcomer should ask who protects those hours when the quarter goes badly.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the learning environment is comparatively kind. Experiments read out in ten days, samples are large, and a junior can be asked to predict the lift before the test is unblinded — a cheap, honest, weekly repetition. The risk is the opposite one: fast feedback on small decisions can produce a junior who is superbly calibrated on button copy and has never held a judgement that took a quarter to resolve.

In B2B and enterprise the environment is wicked. Nine accounts, a sales motion that confounds every signal, and a renewal cycle that returns its verdict twelve months later. Repetitions there must be manufactured: predict which three accounts will escalate this quarter; predict which requirement the security review will reject; write the objection you expect from the customer's IT head before the call. The prediction is cheap and the correction arrives within weeks rather than years.

In marketplaces the specific trap is that supply-side and demand-side judgement are different skills wearing the same job title. A junior who develops good instincts about seller onboarding will generalise them confidently to buyer conversion and be wrong in ways that are hard to see, because both sides move together in the aggregate numbers.

Stage changes the constraint rather than the principle. In an early-stage company there are few seniors to correct anyone, but the market returns verdicts quickly and brutally; learning is fast, high-variance and largely unsupervised, and the junior's main protection is writing predictions down so that the lessons are not reconstructed after the fact. In a large company seniors exist but their attention is rationed, and the environment is so confounded that the counterfactual is almost never visible. That is precisely why the deliberate design of repetitions matters more at scale, and why it is at scale that it is most often skipped.

7. Common mistakes

The polished-draft junior. The symptom from outside is documents that arrive complete and confident, revisions that are purely cosmetic, and a meeting in which the author cannot say why the second option was rejected. The underlying misunderstanding is that the artefact was the thinking. The cheapest diagnostic takes sixty seconds: ask for the strongest case for the option they did not pick. Someone who formed a view will answer immediately; someone who ratified a draft will summarise the draft.

The tool curriculum. The symptom is an onboarding plan that reads as a list of systems, prompt libraries and certifications. The misunderstanding is that fluency distinguishes people. The diagnostic is to ask what the junior will have decided by day ninety, not what they will have used; if the plan cannot name three decisions, it is a software induction.

The unfalsifiable review. The symptom is that juniors "review" generated work and approve essentially all of it. The misunderstanding is that review without prior commitment constitutes evaluation. The diagnostic is documentary: look for any number that was written down before the data was pulled. If the pre-commitment log does not exist, no repetitions are occurring, whatever the process document says.

The quiet exit from apprenticeship. The symptom is a team that stops hiring juniors while saying nothing against them — "we'd rather have one senior" — repeated until the pipeline is gone. The misunderstanding is treating apprenticeship as charity rather than as capital expenditure on the firm's own future bench. The diagnostic question, which Meera put to Arvind directly, is: who will be your senior product managers in 2031, and where do you propose they come from?

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Meera's decision does not look like a new syllabus. It looks like three small, dull mechanisms that survive a bad quarter. First, a pre-commitment log per APM: one page a week, the judgement written before the answer is available, dated. Second, a protected set of hand-built repetitions — at Samvit, ten customer calls attended live with no transcript assistance, on the grounds that raw exposure is the input from which taste is later built and cannot be reconstituted from a summary. Third, a weekly twenty-five-minute "defend the diff": the APM brings the generated draft, their own prior answer, and the argument for the difference, and a senior PM argues the other side. Everything else in a good programme is scaffolding around those three.

9. What Meera decided

On Thursday, 22 January, Meera sent Arvind and the leadership group a four-page note. She kept the cohort at five and cut the twelve-week programme to six, on the argument that the production-shadowing weeks had become ceremonial. She reallocated the four senior PMs' coaching hours from draft correction to the defend-the-diff format, and she costed it honestly: about 200 senior hours a year, roughly ₹34 lakh of loaded senior time, against the cohort's ₹1.1 crore. Her closing argument was the one she had started with in Figure 1. The cohort was never a cheap-labour scheme; it was the firm's only mechanism for manufacturing judgement, and the tools had removed the mechanism without removing the need.

What to learn next follows directly. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill is the thing this topic is trying to manufacture, and it deserves study on its own terms. Reviewing work you did not write is the daily form the repetition takes. Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved explains why the organisation will misread all of this as a productivity story and act accordingly.

Two questions to sit with.

1. In your own last month of work, name one judgement you committed to in writing before you saw the answer. If you cannot, what has been teaching you?

2. If your team stopped hiring juniors tomorrow and nobody complained for three years, what would be the first observable symptom in year four — and could you detect it in year one?

Pranati Payments: The Cohort Question

Lens for this case: what a junior PM should learn first now. If the work that used to teach the craft has been automated, what is a junior for — and what should they be doing on Monday?

1. A Thursday evening in Koramangala

On Thursday, 5 March 2026, at twenty past eight, Aparna Iyer was the last person on the third floor of Pranati Payments' office on 80 Feet Road in Koramangala, Bengaluru. On her screen was a two-page note from Rakesh Nambiar, Pranati's co-founder and chief financial officer, circulated that afternoon to the four members of the executive group. Its recommendation was a single sentence: discontinue the associate product manager programme with effect from the new financial year and redeploy the budget to two senior product hires.

Aparna, Head of Product, had to respond by the executive review on Tuesday, 10 March. She did not have the luxury of arguing in the abstract. On the same Tuesday she also had to name the person who would own discovery for Pranati's largest commitment of the year — an automated collections module promised to Al Ufuq Trading in Dubai for their Ramadan and post-Ramadan buying cycle, with a contractual first delivery on 31 July.

The two decisions were the same decision, and Aparna knew it.

2. Pranati Payments

Pranati was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Rakesh Nambiar and two engineers from a large payments processor, to solve a specific and unglamorous problem: small and mid-sized Indian businesses could accept money easily but could not collect it reliably. Invoices went unpaid, reminders went out by WhatsApp, and reconciliation happened in Tally at month-end. Pranati built a collections layer on top of UPI — recurring mandates through UPI Autopay under the NPCI framework, automatic reminders, GST-compliant invoicing, and a reconciliation feed that matched settlements against invoices without human intervention.

By February 2026 Pranati served 41,000 merchants, processed ₹1,840 crore of collections a quarter, and had annual recurring revenue of ₹96 crore growing at about 34 per cent. It was a small player in a crowded field. Razorpay, Cashfree and PhonePe all offered recurring collections; Paytm and Zoho's finance suite reached overlapping customers; Pranati's defensible position was depth in the mid-market collections workflow rather than breadth in payments. Its largest domestic account was Vaidehi Stores, a 210-outlet grocery chain headquartered in Coimbatore that used Pranati to collect from its franchisees.

The product organisation numbered fourteen: Aparna, three senior product managers, four associate product managers, four designers and two product-operations analysts. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune. The data scientist, Neil D'Souza, worked from Toronto. The design lead, Katharina Weiss, had moved to Berlin in 2023 and stayed. Farida Sheikh ran customer success from Singapore, covering both the ASEAN merchants and the Gulf accounts. Vikram Rao ran sales for the small but growing North American book out of Newark, New Jersey, selling mostly to Indian-origin business owners billing customers in both currencies.

3. The situation

Rakesh's note was not careless. It rested on a set of observations Aparna had herself supplied at the January planning offsite.

Since mid-2025, Pranati had put an internal assistant into the product workflow — connected to its own ticketing system, product analytics and the merchant knowledge base. The effects were large and measurable. Weekly reconciliation-failure summaries, which an APM used to compile in four hours, now arrived automatically at 07:00 on Mondays. Merchant-onboarding documentation, once a two-day job, was regenerated from the API schema in minutes. The support-ticket clustering that APMs had done by hand each fortnight was continuous and better. And a first-draft product requirements document, given three paragraphs of intent, came back in about twenty minutes with a competitive scan, acceptance criteria and a metrics section that was usually defensible.

Rakesh's arithmetic followed. Four APMs cost ₹1.12 crore a year fully loaded. Their output, measured as artefacts shipped, had risen — but so had everyone's. Meanwhile the senior product managers were stretched, and Bengaluru senior PM salaries had risen sharply as Freshworks, Zoho, Razorpay and the larger product companies competed for the same three hundred people. Two strong senior PMs would cost roughly the same ₹1.12 crore and would, in his words, "actually be able to take Al Ufuq off your desk."

What unsettled Aparna was an exercise she had run quietly on 20 February, without telling Rakesh. She had taken a real specification for a UPI Autopay mandate-retry feature, had the assistant redraft it, and then had deliberately planted six defects in the draft — a retry schedule that breached NPCI's permitted mandate-debit window, a success-metric definition that counted a retried collection twice, a missing Data Protection and Digital Privacy Act consent step for storing merchant-side customer contact details, an acceptance criterion that contradicted the one above it, an assumption that Al Ufuq's fiscal calendar matched the Indian one, and a scope item that Katharina's team had already shown to fail in usability testing in November.

She gave the document to all four APMs and, as a control, to two of her three senior PMs, telling each only that it was a draft for review. The results are in Exhibit 3, and they were the reason she had not slept well since.

Farida, from Singapore, had her own view and had stated it on a call at 09:00 IST that Tuesday: "Al Ufuq's finance controller has closed nineteen Ramadan cycles. If we put a person with eleven months of experience in front of him, he will be polite, he will answer every question we ask, and he will not tell us the one thing we did not know to ask. That is not a training problem, Aparna, that is an ₹18 crore account."

Vikram, from Newark, wanted something different again. His North American merchants were asking for dual-currency invoicing, and he had been waiting eleven months for anyone at all to look at it. His position was that the argument about who was learning what was a luxury, and that Pranati simply needed more hands.

4. The people

Aparna Iyer, 38, Head of Product, Bengaluru. Joined Pranati in 2021 from a large enterprise software firm. Built the APM programme herself in 2022 and has promoted two of its graduates. Wants the Al Ufuq delivery to be safe and wants Pranati to still have senior product people in 2031 without paying a hiring premium for all of them.

Rakesh Nambiar, 44, co-founder and CFO, Bengaluru. Carries a board commitment to reach operating breakeven by March 2027. Not hostile to juniors; he simply believes the programme's original rationale — cheap capable hands for necessary work — has been dissolved by the tooling, and that nobody has replaced it with a new rationale that survives a spreadsheet.

Farida Sheikh, 41, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns renewal for Al Ufuq and for eleven other Gulf and ASEAN accounts. Her incentive is squarely on retention. She is the fastest, most specific critic of any requirement document in the company — she replies within a day and her objections come with reasons.

Ishita Bose, 26, Associate Product Manager, Bengaluru, eighteen months in. Ships more documents than any APM Aparna has ever managed. In the 20 February exercise she caught three of the six planted defects — the highest APM score — and took fourteen minutes to do it. Has begun asking Aparna, without quite saying so, whether she is actually getting better at anything.

Exhibit 3 is the piece of evidence that changed the shape of Aparna's problem. Read one way, it supports Rakesh: the APMs cannot catch what matters, so buy seniors. Read another way, it indicts the programme rather than the people — the APMs were fast and confident precisely because nobody had ever asked them to commit to an answer before reading one. The footnote is the finding. Both seniors wrote down what the NPCI mandate window should be before they read the draft's version of it, and both then noticed the discrepancy. The APMs read the draft first and had nothing to compare it against.

6. The options

Option A — Close the cohort, hire two senior PMs. Rakesh's proposal. Al Ufuq gets an experienced owner, Farida is satisfied, Vikram's dual-currency backlog finally moves, and the FY2027 breakeven commitment is easier to defend. The costs are a four-to-six-month hiring lag in a market where Bengaluru senior PMs have three offers, the loss of Pranati's only internal source of future senior product managers, and the immediate departure of Ishita and probably one other APM, who will read the decision correctly.

Option B — Keep all four APMs and lean into throughput. Let the APMs run at the speed the tooling allows: more specifications, more documentation, faster ticket response, no additional senior time. This is the cheapest option and the one that looks best on a quarterly output review. Its cost is invisible for about two years and then total: on the evidence of Exhibit 3, the APMs will continue to ratify drafts they cannot evaluate, and Pranati will have four people with three years of tenure and eighteen months of judgement.

Option C — Cut the cohort to two or three and rebuild it around judgement. Keep Ishita and one other; move the remaining budget to a single senior hire rather than two. Redesign the APM's work so that every substantial artefact begins with a written pre-commitment — the APM's own answer, timestamped, before the draft is opened — and is defended weekly against a senior PM. Put an APM on the Al Ufuq discovery, but route every requirement through Farida in Singapore for objection before it reaches the customer, making her scepticism the feedback loop rather than the obstacle. The costs are real: roughly 200 senior hours a year that will not be spent shipping, a slower first quarter, and a genuine execution risk on a 31 July contractual date with ₹18 crore of revenue behind it.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows APM production work falling from 880 hours to 194. What, precisely, did Pranati lose along with those 686 hours, and where in Exhibit 3 can you see the loss?

2. Rakesh and Aparna agree on every number in Exhibit 2 and disagree on the conclusion. What is the actual point of disagreement, and which row of the exhibit contains it?

3. Farida's objection is about risk on a single account; Aparna's concern is about capability in 2031. How should Aparna weigh a specific, near-term, ₹18 crore risk against a diffuse, long-term one — and is there a design of the work in which she does not have to choose?

4. What should Aparna recommend on Tuesday, 10 March, and what is the first thing the chosen APM or senior PM should do on Monday morning?

8. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is the question of what a junior product manager should learn first now, and its central claim is a distinction. Production is making the artefact. Evaluation is deciding whether the artefact is any good. Specification is deciding what artefact should exist at all. Until recently, juniors acquired evaluation as a free by-product of production: they made things slowly, someone corrected them, and over dozens of corrections their sense of "good" came into calibration. The cost of production has now collapsed. The by-product has gone with it. Nothing has replaced it by default.

That is exactly what Exhibits 1 and 3 show together. Exhibit 1 is the disappearance of the mechanism; Exhibit 3 is the consequence, measured. And the footnote to Exhibit 3 names the operative variable, which is not intelligence or effort but pre-commitment: the seniors wrote their answer down before they read the draft, and the APMs did not. A review conducted after reading a fluent, confident document is not evaluation; it is ratification, and it teaches the reviewer nothing, because the mind that has read the answer cannot recover what it would have thought unaided.

A well-reasoned answer to this case therefore does two things. It refuses the framing that the choice is between juniors and seniors — that framing takes the old programme as given and asks only whether to keep paying for it. And it treats senior attention, not headcount and not tooling, as the scarce input whose allocation must be decided explicitly.

One defensible path is Option C, with three specific commitments. First, cut the cohort to two rather than keeping four, because coaching hours per junior, not the number of juniors, is what produces calibration — two APMs with 100 senior hours each will learn far more than four with 50. Second, put an APM on the Al Ufuq discovery precisely because Farida is difficult: her objections arrive within a day and come with reasons, which makes her the fastest feedback loop available anywhere in the company, and fast, specific feedback is the entire mechanism by which judgement is built. Protect the account by making a senior PM formally accountable for the delivery while the APM owns the discovery — the risk Farida named is real and should be answered with accountability, not with distance. Third, put the coaching cost in the plan as a visible line item, about ₹52 lakh of senior time, because a cost that stays invisible is the first thing cut in a bad quarter, and this one will be tested by June.

Option A is not unreasonable, and a student who argues it should be credited if they say plainly what it forfeits: Pranati becomes permanently dependent on buying senior judgement in the most competitive talent market in India, at a premium that rises every year. Option B is the one to argue against hardest, not because it is obviously wrong on Tuesday, but because it is the only option whose failure will not be visible until 2029.

Tanmatra Systems: Three Point Two Per Cent

A health-claims company automated the work its people learned on, watched every quality metric improve, and then discovered that it could not tell the difference between a machine that had got better and reviewers who had stopped reviewing.

1. Sunday night, Kondapur

On Sunday, 15 March 2026, Nandita Varma sat at the dining table of her flat in Kondapur, Hyderabad, with three documents open and the board pre-read still unsent. The Tanmatra Systems board met at nine the next morning at the office in HITEC City, with two directors dialling in from Mumbai and one from Singapore. The pre-read was due at midnight.

Nandita was Chief Product Officer. She had been at Tanmatra for five years, and in that time the company had gone from eleven customers' worth of pilot work to ₹128 crore of annual recurring revenue adjudicating health insurance claims. The documents on her table were, in order: the remediation report on the Aaditri General Insurance incident, due to the client by 20 March; the FY2027 budget, which locked on 25 March; and the campus offer list for the 2026 intake of what everybody at Tanmatra still called the Academy, on which fourteen offers to graduates of Osmania University, NIT Warangal and two Hyderabad commerce colleges would lapse at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, 18 March.

Three hundred and forty claims had been wrongly repudiated at Aaditri between 5 January and 20 February, worth ₹4.62 crore of cover. Every one of them had been through a human reviewer. Every one of those reviewers had clicked approve. The board would want to know what had gone wrong and what Nandita proposed to do about it, and she had four answers, none of which she believed completely.

2. How Tanmatra got here

Tanmatra Systems was founded in 2018 by Sanjay Varada, who had spent nine years in health-insurance operations, and Leela Kothapalli, who had built risk-scoring systems for a Bengaluru lending company. Their product, Adjudicate, sat between an insurer or third-party administrator and the hospital network: it read claim documents, matched them against the policy wording, applied the insurer's own rules, and produced an adjudication decision with a reasoning note. In 2018 the machine's job was narrow — digitise, classify, flag. Humans decided almost everything.

By March 2026 Tanmatra served nine Indian insurers and TPAs and two in the Gulf, and its customers included Aaditri General Insurance, a mid-sized Mumbai multiline insurer with ₹6,100 crore of gross written premium, and Zarqa Insurance Services in Dubai, which at ₹22 crore of annual contract value was Tanmatra's single largest account. Headcount was 312. Revenue per employee was ₹41 lakh; the Series B investors, who had put in ₹310 crore in 2023, expected ₹65 lakh by FY2028.

The decision that constrains everything happened in 2021. Tanmatra needed people who could read a claim file and tell whether an adjudication was right — a skill the Indian market did not sell in volume at a price a start-up could pay. Sanjay's answer was to build it. The Academy hired commerce graduates from tier-two cities, trained them for eleven weeks on policy wordings, exclusions, IRDAI regulation and the anatomy of a hospital bill, and put them on live claims under supervision. They were called claims analysts. They audited the machine's output, and the disputes they had with it became the company's training data.

The Academy turned out to be more than a staffing solution. Six of Tanmatra's current eleven product managers came out of it, including two of three group PMs. Devika Rane, who joined the 2021 cohort at twenty-three from a Nanded commerce college, was now Group PM for the adjudication engine in Pune. Nobody had planned this. Analysts spent two years arguing with a model about claims and came out with an intuition for the product that no lateral hire seemed to acquire.

The second consequence of 2021 was contractual, and it is the harder one. When Tanmatra signed Zarqa in 2024, the differentiator it sold was not the model. It was the guarantee that a trained human would review every flagged claim within four hours, Gulf business hours, at a 95 per cent service level, with penalties of 2 per cent of the quarterly fee per breached percentage point up to a cap of 10 per cent. That human review was staffed from the analyst pool. The Academy is therefore simultaneously Tanmatra's leadership pipeline and a delivery obligation written into its largest contract, and any decision about one is a decision about the other.

3. The industry around it

Indian health insurance in 2026 was growing fast and under close regulatory attention. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India had, through its master circular on health insurance and the Cashless Everywhere framework, tightened expectations on turnaround times for cashless authorisation and on the handling of repudiated claims, including grievance redressal timelines and escalation to the Insurance Ombudsman. Insurers faced published claim-settlement ratios and a public that had learned to read them. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had come into force with its rules, and health data sat squarely in its most sensitive band, which mattered a great deal to a company whose product improved by learning from claim documents.

Tanmatra's competition came from three directions. Established Indian technology services firms — Infosys, TCS and their peers — sold adjudication modernisation as part of larger core-insurance programmes and could out-resource Tanmatra on any single deal. Product companies such as Freshworks and Zoho were not competitors but were fierce competitors for the same Hyderabad and Bengaluru engineering and product talent. And the insurers themselves — the large private players and the newer digital-first ones — increasingly built in-house, which made Tanmatra's proposition less "we have a model" and more "we have people who know claims."

The Gulf exposure changed the shape of the business again. Zarqa's book was a mix of group medical for expatriate workforces and retail cover, with a different regulator, different policy wordings, a Ramadan and post-Ramadan seasonality that had nothing to do with the Indian claim calendar, and an expectation of English-language reasoning notes that a Dubai compliance officer could read. Raymond Coelho, Tanmatra's head of sales in New Jersey, was meanwhile eleven weeks into diligence on a $2.4 million pilot with a US health payer, where the selling story was automation depth, not human review.

4. The situation, in sequence

What follows is the sequence as Tanmatra reconstructed it in the first week of March, together with what was believed at each point.

November 2024. Leela's team built the evaluation suite for Adjudicate: 4,180 historical claims with adjudications agreed by two senior analysts, spanning nine claim categories. It was the artefact Tanmatra showed customers. Belief at the time: a fixed, high-quality benchmark is the right way to measure a claims model, and refreshing it often would make scores incomparable across releases.

March 2025. The copilot went to every reviewer. It read the file, retrieved the applicable policy clauses, drafted the adjudication decision and wrote the reasoning note. The reviewer's screen showed the draft decision at the top, the evidence below, and two buttons. Belief: reviewers would read the evidence and use the draft as a starting point.

August 2025. Two things happened in the same fortnight. The FY2026 mid-year review halved Academy intake from sixteen to eight, on Nandita's recommendation, on the argument that copilot-era analysts were four times as productive and the company needed revenue per employee to move. And Anneke Brandt, design lead in Berlin, circulated a proposal for a revised review screen that would ask the reviewer to record their own decision before the draft was revealed. It was estimated at nine engineering weeks and deprioritised in favour of the Zarqa Arabic-language reasoning notes. Belief: the review screen was a usability question, not a quality question.

October 2025. Aaditri adopted revised policy wordings across three retail health products, aligning with the current regulatory framework. Tanmatra's clause-retrieval index was updated with the new documents on 14 October. The eval suite was not touched; it still contained only 2023 and 2024 claims under the previous wordings.

5 January to 20 February 2026. Three hundred and forty claims under one of the revised products were repudiated on a ground that the new wording no longer supported. The copilot retrieved a clause from the correct document but applied an exclusion whose scope had narrowed; its reasoning note was fluent, cited the right document and the right section number, and was wrong. Reviewers approved 336 of the 340 within a median of 2.4 minutes.

21 February. Aaditri's grievance team noticed a cluster. Prakash Iyengar, their head of claims operations, called Sanjay directly.

What has since turned out to be wrong. Three beliefs failed. The eval suite was not measuring the live system: its score rose while field accuracy on newly-worded products fell, because it contained no post-revision claims and could not have detected the failure. The productivity gain was not unambiguous: review time per flagged claim had fallen from 11.0 minutes to 2.6, and the override rate — the share of drafts a reviewer changed — from 18.4 per cent to 3.2 per cent, and Tanmatra had read the second number as evidence of model quality when it is equally consistent with reviewers ceasing to review. And the assumption that Academy graduates and lateral hires were interchangeable had never been tested until the first week of March, when Nandita tested it, with results that were suggestive and badly confounded.

5. The people

Nandita Varma, 41, Chief Product Officer, Hyderabad. Owns the copilot roadmap and the Academy. Her stated position is that the incident is a systems failure with several causes and should not be reduced to one. Her incentive is to hold the product organisation together through a Series C process. What she is not saying: she personally recommended halving the Academy intake in August, she signed off on freezing the eval suite in November 2024, and she was the person who deprioritised Anneke's review-screen proposal.

Sanjay Varada, 47, co-founder and CEO, Hyderabad. Position: fix it fast, keep the Gulf and US expansion on track, do not reopen settled decisions in front of the board. Incentive: a live Series C conversation at ₹1,850 crore pre-money in which revenue per employee is an explicit diligence item. Not saying: the term sheet has a headcount-efficiency milestone attached to the second tranche.

Leela Kothapalli, 44, co-founder and CTO, Hyderabad. Position: this is a data-freshness bug; refresh the index and the eval corpus, add a wording-change detector, and the class of failure closes. Incentive: her team built both the copilot and the suite. Not saying: she raised the staleness of the eval corpus once, in a written thread on 9 September 2025, and nobody replied, and she did not raise it again.

Devika Rane, 28, Group PM, adjudication engine, Pune, Academy class of 2021. Position: restore the Academy at full intake and rebuild the analyst path, because it is the only mechanism that has ever produced a Tanmatra product manager who can read a claim. Incentive: it is her own origin, and she says so openly. Not saying: two of her strongest analysts have accepted offers from a large IT services firm at a 40 per cent increase, and she has not yet told Nandita.

Meher Contractor, 39, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: put senior reviewers on Zarqa immediately and do not let the incident travel. Incentive: the Zarqa renewal falls in her number. Not saying: Zarqa's operations head asked her, in a corridor conversation in February, what she thought of a competing product, and she has not reported it.

Raymond Coelho, 52, Head of Sales, North America, Newark, New Jersey. Position: the answer is more automation, not less; the US payer pilot is being sold on straight-through processing rates and any story involving more human reviewers is a story about higher cost. Incentive: commission on a $2.4 million pilot. Not saying: the deck he has been presenting since January shows a straight-through rate that the product organisation has not agreed to.

Aarav Khandelwal, 33, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the override rate is uninterpretable as currently measured, and Tanmatra should run an interleaved audit — routing a hidden random sample of claims to two independent reviewers and to a blind senior adjudicator — before drawing any conclusion at all. Incentive: methodological rigour, and a paper he would like to write. Not saying: he ran an unauthorised version of that audit on 180 claims in December 2025 and the results were worse than February's, and he has not circulated them because the sample was drawn in a way he could not defend.

Anneke Brandt, 36, Design Lead, Berlin. Position: the review screen is the proximate cause, because it shows the answer before it asks the question, and no staffing decision will fix an interface that makes ratification the path of least resistance. Incentive: an expanded remit for design in the review experience. Not saying: her August proposal would have added roughly forty seconds per claim, which at current volumes breaches the Zarqa four-hour service level unless headcount rises.

Prakash Iyengar, 55, Head of Claims Operations, Aaditri General Insurance, Mumbai. Position: he wants the remediation completed, a written root-cause account he can put into his own grievance reporting, and assurance on the other two revised products. Incentive: his own accountability to his board and to the regulator on grievance metrics. Not saying: Aaditri reduced its internal claims review team by eighteen positions in 2025 on the strength of Tanmatra's automation, and that decision is his.

Stop the Academy, and hire eight to ten experienced claims adjudicators from the insurance industry in Mumbai and Hyderabad at roughly ₹18 to ₹24 lakh each — call it ₹1.7 crore a year — to sit over the review pool as senior arbiters. The struck-through line said: "or is the question who reviews at all?" 9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board pre-read is due at midnight on Sunday, 15 March, and the meeting is at nine on Monday. Fourteen campus offers lapse at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, 18 March; the colleges will not hold placements open past that. Aaditri's root-cause report and the remaining 72 reinstatements are due to Prakash by 20 March, and his own grievance reporting cycle runs behind that. The FY2027 budget locks on 25 March with an incremental spending authority of ₹14 crore across the whole company, most of which is already committed to the Gulf delivery team. The Zarqa contract's service-level terms can be renegotiated only in the window ending 31 March, and Meher has not yet told anyone that Zarqa's operations head has been looking elsewhere.

Two constraints are less visible. Refreshing the eval corpus with recent claims is not simply an engineering task: under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, using policyholder health documents for a purpose beyond adjudication requires a lawful basis that Tanmatra's contracts with two of its nine Indian customers do not currently establish, and legal has estimated six to nine weeks to paper it. And Tanmatra has never once measured what it would most need to know — whether a reviewer who records a decision before seeing the draft catches more errors than one who does not — because until August 2025 nobody thought it was a question, and after August 2025 it was nine engineering weeks that belonged to Zarqa.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 3 shows the override rate falling from 18.4 per cent to 3.2 per cent. List every explanation consistent with that fall. What measurement would distinguish between them, and why does Tanmatra not have it?

2. Exhibit 2 contains three accuracy numbers that disagree. For each, state precisely what it measures and what it cannot measure. If you had to give the board one number on Monday, which would you give and how would you caveat it?

3. Exhibit 5 is the only direct evidence about the Academy, and its author lists four confounds. How much weight does it deserve? What would a version of that audit look like that a sceptic could not dismiss, and could Tanmatra run it before 18 March?

4. Leela says it is not a people problem; Devika says the 336 approvals are the whole problem; Anneke says it is the screen. These are not mutually exclusive. Construct the causal account that accommodates all three, and say which link in it Tanmatra could actually intervene on this quarter.

5. The Academy is simultaneously a training pipeline, a cost line and a contractual delivery obligation to Zarqa. Whose decision should it be, and what does it say about Tanmatra that the FY2027 analyst headcount was set to hit a revenue-per-employee milestone before anyone checked it against Exhibit 6?

6. What should Nandita do on Monday morning — and what, exactly, should she say to the board about why 336 trained reviewers approved 336 wrong decisions, in a median of two minutes and twenty-four seconds each?

Half past eleven

At half past eleven the pre-read was still a draft. Nandita had written and deleted the same opening paragraph four times. The first version began with the incident. The second began with the fix. The third began with the Academy, and she deleted it because she could hear Sanjay's voice in the corridor saying bring it to me in April with a number attached, and she did not have a number.

The fourth version began with a question, which she knew was not how one writes to a board. It read: "Our reviewers spent 2.4 minutes on each of 340 claims and agreed with the machine 336 times. We do not currently know whether that is because the machine was right, or because we have built a system in which a person who has already read the answer cannot be expected to disagree with it. I would like to tell you which, and I cannot."

Outside, the Kondapur traffic had thinned. Devika had sent a message at eleven that said only: the offers lapse Wednesday. Aarav's three-week audit would report on 3 April. The board met in nine and a half hours.

What a junior PM should learn first now

The tasks juniors learned the craft on can now be automated. The craft cannot. This page is about the gap between those two sentences, and about the fact that nobody has yet closed it.

1. Two rooms, the same week

On Tuesday, 3 March 2026, Rhea Kamath had a spreadsheet open on the eighth floor of Udgam Money's office at One Lodha Place in Lower Parel, Mumbai, and a deadline of Friday, 20 March. Udgam was a consumer money app — UPI payments layered over a savings and micro-investing product, 7.2 million monthly active users, ₹910 crore of assets under a mutual-fund distribution licence, and a product organisation of thirty-one people. Rhea, VP of Product, had to submit the FY2026-27 hiring plan: ₹6.4 crore of product headcount, currently proposed as nine associate product managers and four senior hires.

The finance committee had asked a reasonable question at the January review. Udgam's APM cohort had been created in 2021, when a single funnel analysis took an APM three days. By early 2026, the same analysis — cohorted, segmented by acquisition channel, with a written interpretation — came back from Udgam's internal analytics assistant in about eleven minutes, and the APMs' role in it was to read the output and forward it. The committee's question was blunt: what exactly are nine APMs for?

Four hundred and fifty kilometres away in Baner, Pune, Kunal Deshpande faced a narrower version of the same question with higher immediate stakes. Kunal was Head of Product at Dakshata Systems, which sold supply-chain planning software to 140 enterprise customers — large FMCG manufacturers, two automotive tier-one suppliers, a pharmaceutical distributor — at ₹210 crore of annual recurring revenue. Dakshata's largest account outside India was Al Tayseer Retail Group in Dubai, ₹18 crore a year, and Al Tayseer had asked for a promotions-forecasting module by the September 2026 festive and Ramadan planning cycle.

Kunal had two APMs, Nikhil Sathe and Divya Rangan, seventeen and eleven months into the role. He wanted to give them the discovery for that module. Shirin Dastur, Dakshata's customer-success lead in Singapore, had written to him on 27 February to object, in terms he found difficult to dismiss: "Al Tayseer's planning head has been doing this for nineteen years. If we send two people who have never lived a festive season stock-out to scope it, we will get a beautiful document and the wrong product, and I will be the one in the room in October."

Both decisions turn on one unresolved question. The tasks on which product managers historically acquired judgement have become cheap. The judgement has not. Whether judgement can still be acquired — and if so, through what — is the subject of this page, and it is genuinely unsettled.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Begin with a distinction that the old apprenticeship bundled so tightly that few people separated it.

Production is making the artefact — the requirements document, the funnel analysis, the synthesis of thirty interviews, the competitive scan. Evaluation is deciding whether the artefact in front of you is sound: whether the analysis holds, whether the requirement is the right requirement, whether the synthesis has discarded the one sentence that mattered. Specification is deciding which artefact should exist at all — which question is worth a quarter of the organisation's attention.

Until roughly 2023, evaluation was acquired almost entirely as a by-product of production. A junior wrote the thing slowly and imperfectly; a senior corrected it; after thirty or forty iterations the junior's sense of "good" drifted into calibration with someone whose calibration was already worth something. Nobody designed this arrangement and no company costed it, because the production had to be done by somebody and juniors were the cheapest somebody available. Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger gave the general pattern its name in 1991 — legitimate peripheral participation, in which newcomers learn a craft by performing real but low-consequence parts of the real work at its edge. Kenneth Arrow had given it its economics thirty years earlier in "The Economic Implications of Learning by Doing" (1962): capability accumulates as a function of cumulative output, not of elapsed time.

The intellectual history of why this matters when the periphery is automated runs through a small, unusually durable literature. Michael Polanyi's Personal Knowledge (1958) established that a great deal of expert knowledge is tacit — we know more than we can tell — and therefore cannot be transferred by document. William Chase and Herbert Simon's chess studies (1973) gave that tacit knowledge a mechanism: expertise is largely a very large library of recognised patterns, accumulated over roughly a decade of exposure. K. Anders Ericsson's work on deliberate practice (1993) added the crucial qualifier that mere repetition builds nothing; repetition at the edge of current ability, with prompt and specific feedback, builds a great deal. Robin Hogarth's Educating Intuition (2001) distinguished kind learning environments, where feedback is fast, accurate and unambiguous, from wicked ones, where it is delayed, noisy and confounded, and showed that intuition calibrates only in the former. Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein, in their 2009 adversarial collaboration "Conditions for Intuitive Expertise", reduced the whole question to two tests: does the environment have enough regularity to be learnable, and does the practitioner get enough practice with feedback to learn it?

And the mechanism by which automation damages this is older than any of the AI discussion. Lisanne Bainbridge's "Ironies of Automation" (1983) observed that automating the routine portions of a task removes precisely the practice that built the skill the operator needs for the non-routine portions, leaving a human who is responsible only for the hard cases and has had no way of becoming good at them. Every serious version of the present argument is a restatement of Bainbridge in a product organisation.

So far, so agreed. Where competent practitioners genuinely part company is on what follows. Four positions are worth stating precisely, because most workplace arguments about junior hiring are two of these talking past each other.
