3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practitioners who take this seriously converge on a small machine with four moving parts. The third part is the one that is almost always left implicit, and its absence is why most well-intentioned programmes produce nothing.

The task ledger. Enumerate every artefact a junior would have produced in their first twelve months. Mark each as production, evaluation or specification. Against each, record the hours it took in 2021 and the hours it takes now. The difference is not a productivity gain to be banked; it is a quantity of learning that has left the organisation without appearing on any report.

The feedback audit. For each remaining task, record three properties of the feedback it generates: latency (how long until the world returns a verdict), attributability (whether the verdict can be traced to this decision rather than to four others), and resolution (whether the verdict distinguishes "right" from "roughly right"). Hogarth's kind/wicked distinction is exactly this triple. A product surface with ten-day experiment readouts and stable traffic is kind. An enterprise roadmap with a twelve-month renewal cycle and a sales motion on top of it is wicked, and no amount of tooling makes it kind.

The pre-commitment. A repetition teaches only if the learner committed to a judgement before the answer was available. Reading a generated draft and approving it is not evaluation; it is ratification, and it teaches nothing, because a mind that has read a fluent, confident document cannot recover what it would have concluded unaided. This is anchoring, and it is not defeated by instructing people not to anchor. The remedy is procedural: the junior writes their own answer first — the number they expect, the requirement they would cut, the option they would choose and the reason — with a timestamp, and only then opens the draft. Their deliverable is the difference between the two and the argument for it.

The senior attention budget. Correcting prose and analysis is now largely unnecessary; the prose is fine and the analysis is competently structured. The same senior hours can be spent on judgement instead. Senior attention, not tooling and not the junior's effort, is the binding constraint, and its arithmetic determines nearly everything else.

The quantitative treatment

There is a usable, honest, approximate model. Define a calibrated repetition as one instance in which a junior committed in writing to a judgement and then received a specific correction from someone better calibrated. Let R be the annual count of such repetitions:

R = (H × 60) ÷ t, where H is senior coaching hours available per junior per year and t is minutes of senior time per repetition.

Not every repetition carries information. Let q be the probability that the feedback is diagnostic — that the junior can tell why they were wrong, not merely that they were. In a kind environment, q runs about 0.7 to 0.8; in a wicked one, 0.2 to 0.3. Effective repetitions are Reff = R × q.

Finally, assume calibration improves with diminishing returns, which every study from Chase and Simon onward supports:

a(n) = a∞ − (a∞ − a0) e−n/k

where a is the probability of making the right call on a contested judgement, a0 is the untrained base rate, a∞ the ceiling for that surface, and k the number of repetitions to close roughly 63 per cent of the gap. Rhea used a0 = 0.40, a∞ = 0.85, k = 60 — figures she took from Udgam's own experiment-prediction records rather than from literature, which is the only defensible way to set them.

Apply it to both companies. Udgam has six senior PMs who can each protect three hours a week across forty-four working weeks: 6 × 3 × 44 = 792 hours, spread over nine APMs, so H = 88. At t = 20 minutes, R = 264. Udgam's surfaces are kind — weekly experiment readouts on 7.2 million users — so q = 0.75 and Reff = 198. Then a(198) = 0.85 − 0.45 e−3.30 = 0.85 − 0.45(0.0369) = 0.833.

Dakshata has three senior PMs who can protect two hours a week: 3 × 2 × 44 = 264 hours over two APMs, so H = 132 — half again as much personal attention per junior as Udgam offers. R = 396. But the environment is wicked: enterprise renewals, nine-month implementation cycles, outcomes confounded by the customer's own operations. At q = 0.25, Reff = 99, and a(99) = 0.85 − 0.45 e−1.65 = 0.85 − 0.45(0.192) = 0.764.

The inversion is the point and it is counter-intuitive: the small enterprise company that gives its juniors far more senior attention produces less calibration than the large consumer company that gives them less, because the environment throws away three-quarters of the signal. For reference, the 2019 apprenticeship at roughly thirty repetitions a year for three years reaches a(90) = 0.75, and a 2026 programme left textually unchanged while the tools changed underneath it — where pre-commitment has quietly disappeared and perhaps eight repetitions a year survive — reaches a(24) = 0.55 after three years. That last number is the one worth staring at.

Second-order effects

Three consequences follow that most programmes discover only after a year.

The first is a congestion effect. If juniors become individually more productive, the natural response is to hire more of them; but H is senior hours divided by junior headcount, so the mechanism that makes the programme work degrades exactly as the programme succeeds. Udgam's own model told Rhea that at fourteen APMs rather than nine, H falls to 57, Reff to 128, and a to 0.80 — a modest-looking drop that compounds over three years.

The second is senior deskilling. Seniors who stop reviewing drafts stop touching the material. Within eighteen months their own calibration begins to drift, and — this is the uncomfortable part — they too begin deferring to the generated draft, at which point the correction the junior receives is not a correction at all. Bainbridge's irony applies one level up, and almost nobody instruments for it.

The third is Goodhart's law on the prediction log. The moment pre-commitments are visible to performance management, juniors hedge. Stated confidence compresses toward the middle, predictions acquire escape clauses, and the log continues to exist while carrying no information. This is not a hypothetical failure; it is the one Udgam actually had, and Section 8 gives its numbers.

4. When the idea applies, and when it is misleading

State the conditions as claims that can be tested rather than as advice.

Claim 1: production cost for the artefacts your juniors would have produced has fallen by more than roughly five times. At Udgam this is plainly true — funnel analysis from three days to eleven minutes, competitive scans from two days to under an hour. At Dakshata it is only partly true. General-purpose assistants draft a supply-chain planning specification about twice as fast as Nikhil did unaided, not ten times, because the domain vocabulary, the customer's own planning calendar and the integration constraints with SAP-side master data are not in the model's general knowledge. Where production has fallen 2× rather than 10×, the old apprenticeship is damaged but not destroyed, and ripping it out is an overcorrection.

Claim 2: the environment returns attributable verdicts within a quarter. True at Udgam; false at Dakshata, where the September module will not be judged until the March 2027 renewal, by which time Al Tayseer's own merchandising reorganisation will have confounded everything. When this claim is false, calibrated repetitions must be manufactured against proxies rather than outcomes, which is possible but requires deliberate design.

Claim 3: senior capacity exists and is protected against the quarter. Both companies pass on paper and neither has tested it. The honest form of the test is: in the last bad quarter, what happened to coaching hours? At Udgam, in the quarter after the September 2025 UPI-outage incident, coaching hours went to zero for seven weeks and nobody recorded it.

Claim 4: the surface is stable enough that calibration built this year is still worth something next year. This fails in rapidly restructuring product lines and in AI-native features whose behaviour changes when an underlying model is replaced. Calibration against a model's failure modes can be obsoleted overnight by a version upgrade, which is a genuinely new phenomenon with no good precedent.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. First, where the firm's binding constraint is distribution rather than product judgement — a company losing on channel economics does not have a junior-training problem, and reorganising its APM programme is displacement activity. Second, where the junior role is in substance a coverage role: someone has to be reachable at 2 a.m. when the NPCI settlement window misbehaves, and dressing that up as apprenticeship insults everybody. Third, in heavily codified regulatory domains, where a large share of what looks like judgement is written down in a circular — in RBI's digital lending guidelines, in SEBI's advertising code — and can be learned by reading. There, production training genuinely is the training, and the sophisticated argument is the wrong one.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product organisations. Calibration is surface-specific; rotation destroys it. Rotation programmes were designed in an era when breadth was expensive and depth was free — a junior got depth automatically by grinding through production work, so the programme supplied the missing breadth. Now the economics are reversed and most rotation programmes have not noticed. The seam shows up as a PM who is credibly excellent for six weeks after each move and then is not, and whose managers attribute the dip to "ramp" rather than to decalibration.

Two-sided marketplaces. Supply-side and demand-side judgement are different skills that share a job title and a dashboard. A junior who builds real instincts about seller onboarding will transfer them confidently to buyer conversion and be wrong in ways that are hard to detect, because both sides move together in aggregate GMV. The discipline that catches it is forcing the pre-commitment to be side-specific: predict the seller metric and the buyer metric separately, and score them separately.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance and broking, a junior can be genuinely productive in month two because much of the decision space is constrained by RBI, IRDAI or SEBI rules that are legible and teachable. The risk is that they acquire regulatory fluency and mistake it for product judgement — and so do their managers, because regulatory fluency is highly visible and product judgement is not. The tell is a PM who can say what is permitted with great precision and cannot say what is worth doing.

Hardware plus software. Feedback latency is set by tooling and certification cycles measured in eighteen months, so hardware organisations never had fast loops to lose. What they built instead — design reviews where juniors sit in the room, state a position, and hear it dismantled by someone with twenty years of failure modes — is precisely the mechanism software organisations are now rediscovering. Ather's and Mahindra's engineering cultures did not invent the design review for this reason, but it is why the practice transfers.

AI-native products. Here the relationship inverts in an interesting way. The central craft skill in an AI product is designing the evaluation: choosing the cases, writing the rubric, deciding what "good" means when output is probabilistic. That is evaluation skill applied directly, which means a junior with good evaluative instincts is immediately and visibly valuable — the gap between junior and senior is narrower than anywhere else. The failure mode is eval theatre: a large, growing, automatically-scored eval suite that everyone trusts and nobody has read, in which the rubric encodes last quarter's assumptions and the score rises while the product gets worse.

What happens at the organisational seams. What mature companies say is that they have an AI-first APM programme with a modern curriculum. What they mostly do is quietly shrink the cohort, retitle some junior roles as "product engineer" or "product operations" where the output is measurable, and rely on hiring three-to-five-year PMs from competitors who are still, for now, training them. The calibration work that does happen tends to happen informally, inside the one-to-ones of one or two senior people who happen to care about it, and it disappears entirely when those people leave. An organisation's real position on this question is visible not in its curriculum but in what survives its worst quarter.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Ratification wearing the clothes of review

The expert's tell is not revision volume but revision depth. A junior who is genuinely evaluating produces diffs that change conclusions, cut sections and add a paragraph explaining why an option was rejected. A junior who is ratifying produces diffs that change adjectives. The obvious reading — "they made forty edits, they engaged deeply" — is wrong, and edit counts are the metric most likely to be reported upward.

Fluency is read as competence, especially in hiring

An excellent take-home exercise now carries almost no signal about the candidate, because the artefact costs nothing. The expert reads a different variable: what would change your mind, and what did you consider and reject. A candidate who cannot name a serious alternative to their own recommendation has told you they did not generate one.

A repetition without pre-commitment is worth zero, not a little

Practitioners routinely treat this as a matter of degree — "well, they at least read it critically." Anchoring does not work that way. Once a fluent answer is in view, the unaided answer is unrecoverable, and the junior's subsequent agreement carries no information about their judgement. The expert therefore treats the timestamp on the pre-commitment as the thing that makes the exercise exist at all.

The prediction log dies the moment it is graded

The expert's sign is statistical: stated confidence values clustering in a narrow band around 70 to 80 per cent, and predictions acquiring conditional clauses. The obvious reading is that the juniors are becoming appropriately humble. The correct reading is that they have discovered the log is being read by someone who decides their rating, and are optimising for unfalsifiability.

Senior calibration decays too, and nobody measures it

The tell is asking a senior PM when they last personally pulled a cohort or sat through three unfiltered customer calls. If the answer is more than a year, their corrections are running on memory of a product that has changed. The obvious reading — seniority is a stock, not a flow — is exactly wrong; calibration is a flow and it depreciates.

Taste is domain-specific and its decay is invisible

Expert managers watch for the six-week pattern after a surface change: a period of confident, well-argued, slightly wrong calls. Everyone attributes the dip to ramp-up on the new domain's facts. In fact it is the previous domain's priors still firing, and the cure is not more documentation but more pre-committed predictions scored against the new surface.

The scarcity is calibration, not seniority

The most reliably calibrated person in a room is often someone with four years of concentrated exposure to one surface, and the least reliable is often the most senior person present, whose surface was different. Experts notice who has actually been scored, and defer accordingly; competent practitioners defer to title.

Advice about this topic is usually autobiography

Almost everyone senior enough to have an opinion was trained under the old regime, and their intuition — "I learned it fine by grinding" — is a survivorship claim from a sample of one, drawn from a mechanism that no longer exists. The expert discounts confident prescriptions from people who have never watched a cohort trained the new way, including prescriptions in this direction.

The apprenticeship externality is real and it is not your firm's fault

Following Becker, the firm captures only part of the value of general training, so under-investment is individually rational and collectively destructive. The expert recognises this as a coordination problem — one that in other professions was solved by institutions, from chartered accountancy articleship to medical residency — and stops treating individual firms as villains.

Nobody knows the timeline, and confident numbers are the weakest part of any case

No cohort has yet completed an AI-native apprenticeship and reached genuine seniority. Every stated duration — "two years instead of five", "it will take longer, not shorter" — is extrapolation from a curve that no longer applies. The expert's tell is that they will name the uncertainty explicitly and design for being wrong in either direction.

7. Across product types and company stages

In consumer products the environment is comparatively kind: experiments read out in days, samples are large, and metric prediction gives a junior a cheap weekly repetition with honest scoring. The specific risk is narrowness — a PM beautifully calibrated on onboarding copy who has never held a judgement that took two quarters to resolve.

In B2B and enterprise the environment is wicked and the repetitions must be manufactured against proxies: predict which three accounts will escalate this quarter; predict which requirement the customer's security review will reject; write down the objection you expect from their IT head before the call. Each of these returns a verdict in weeks rather than a year, and each is scorable. This is the single highest-leverage move available to a company in Dakshata's position, and it costs almost nothing.

In platforms and marketplaces the difference is the side-specificity described above; in hardware, the difference is that the design-review mechanism substitutes for the feedback loop and always did. In AI products the difference is real and large: evaluation design is both the training and the work.

By stage, the constraint changes rather than the principle. In an early-stage company there are no seniors to correct anyone, but the market returns verdicts fast and hard; learning is quick, high-variance and unsupervised, and the junior's only real protection is writing predictions down so lessons are not reconstructed favourably after the fact. In a large company seniors exist but their attention is rationed and the environment is so confounded that the counterfactual is rarely visible — which is why deliberate design matters most at scale and is most often skipped there. It is worth saying plainly where the difference is not real: the core mechanism — commit, be corrected, repeat — is identical everywhere, and organisations that claim their context is too special for it are usually describing a shortage of senior willingness rather than a structural difference.

8. Three worked examples

Example one: Udgam's metric ladder

From April 2026 Rhea gave each APM a standing weekly obligation: before any experiment readout, write the predicted lift and a confidence, and before any monthly cohort review, write the predicted 30-day retention for the newest cohort. Udgam ran 46 experiments in the first two quarters. Each APM therefore logged roughly 46 predictions, scored automatically, at a senior-time cost of about four minutes per week per APM for the correction conversation, plus the 20-minute deep repetitions already budgeted. The first-quarter results were unflattering and useful: across nine APMs, 414 predictions, median stated confidence 74 per cent, realised accuracy 58 per cent — an overconfidence gap of 16 points. By the second quarter the gap was 9 points. Nothing about the product changed; the APMs simply found out, weekly, that they were wrong, which is the entire mechanism.

Example two: Dakshata manufacturing repetitions in a wicked environment

Kunal could not make renewals faster, so he built proxies. Each Monday, Nikhil and Divya each wrote three predictions: which support ticket category would spike that week, which of four named accounts would raise a P1, and which requirement in the live specification Shirin would object to. Shirin's objections were the valuable one, because they arrived within days and came with reasoning. Over eleven weeks, Divya went from correctly anticipating 4 of 11 objections to 8 of 11. Kunal's estimate was that this raised q from about 0.25 to about 0.45 for that slice of work, which on the model of Section 3 lifts Reff from 99 to 178 and a from 0.764 to 0.827 — larger than anything he could have bought by hiring. The estimate is soft. The direction is not.

Example three: the attempt that failed, and the recovery

Udgam had tried this before. In May 2025, Rhea's predecessor launched an "AI-first APM programme" whose centrepiece was a shared prediction log — and, fatally, made the log an input to the half-yearly performance rating. Over twenty weeks the nine APMs logged 320 predictions. An audit of the first 40 found 11 that were unfalsifiable as written ("retention should improve materially if the cohort composition is stable"). Median stated confidence was 82 per cent against realised accuracy of 61 per cent, a 21-point gap that widened over the period rather than narrowing, which is the signature of hedging rather than of learning. Three of the nine APMs left within seven months against an organisational attrition rate of about 14 per cent a year. The programme was quietly stopped in December 2025.

The recovery had three parts, and the order mattered. First, the log was decoupled from ratings entirely and made visible only to the APM and their coaching senior — which cost the organisation its dashboard and was the price of getting information back. Second, predictions were converted to forced binary or three-way choices with a stated probability, so that unfalsifiable phrasing became impossible. Third, the correction conversation was separated in time from any evaluative conversation by at least two weeks. In the first quarter after the restart, median confidence fell to 66 per cent and realised accuracy rose to 71 per cent — a five-point gap in the other direction, which is roughly where a healthy log sits.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The Compression case, steelmanned. Its strongest form is not that production does not matter but that exposure to outcomes is the active ingredient, and hand-production was merely the historically available vehicle for it. The evidence it rests on is the observation, which anyone can check, that the best juniors have always been the ones with the most contact with real decisions rather than the most output — and that intensive, feedback-rich instruction beats slow accumulation in every domain where the comparison has been run properly, from aviation simulators to surgical training. What would have to be true for it to be wrong: that the act of constructing an argument yourself installs something that observing a constructed argument does not. That is a specific psychological claim, and it is testable in principle.

The Substrate case, steelmanned. Its strongest form is that expert evaluation works by pattern-matching against an internal catalogue of errors, and that the catalogue is built from errors one has personally made and been embarrassed by, not errors one has read about. The evidence is the reliability with which experienced reviewers spot flaws they cannot articulate a rule for, and the well-documented difficulty of teaching debugging, editing or clinical diagnosis from worked examples alone. What would have to be true for it to be wrong: that a catalogue built by evaluating others' work is functionally equivalent to one built by making one's own mistakes. Editors who never wrote, and critics who never performed, are the natural counter-examples, and it is genuinely unclear whether they are good ones.

The Restructuring case, steelmanned. Its strongest form concedes everything about judgement and denies only that the target should be the 2019 senior PM. If the work increasingly consists of specifying problems precisely and evaluating generated solutions, then training people to do that directly — rather than re-creating a ladder whose rungs happened to be assembly work — is simply correct. Its evidence is historical: nearly every craft that was partly automated ended with a different, usually smaller and more judgement-dense profession, and the transitional generation that was trained for the old profile did worst. What would have to be true for it to be wrong: that the old sequence was load-bearing rather than incidental — that you get to specification only by way of production. That is the Substrate claim again, which is why these two schools argue so persistently and so unproductively.

The Pipeline-economics case, steelmanned. Its strongest form is indifferent to all of the above. Whatever the correct pedagogy, no firm will fund general training it cannot capture, so the equilibrium is under-provision regardless, and the interesting question is institutional: whether business schools, professional bodies or structured multi-firm programmes will take up the role that articleship took in accountancy and residency in medicine. Its evidence is the entire history of apprenticeship regulation. What would have to be true for it to be wrong: that firm-specific calibration is a large enough share of the total that firms capture most of the value — plausible, and currently unmeasured.

Nothing in this page resolves these. A synthesis that says "of course it's a bit of all four" is worse than useless, because the four imply materially different hiring plans, and Rhea and Kunal each have to pick one.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask about feedback before they ask about tasks — when a junior joins their team, the first thing they design is how the junior will find out they were wrong, not what the junior will do. They protect coaching hours in writing and treat cancelling them as an incident to be recorded, because they know the mechanism dies quietly. They refuse to read a generated draft before writing their own answer, including for their own work, and they say so out loud, which is what makes the practice spread. And they hold the timeline question open: they can say "we believe this produces calibration in about eighteen months and we do not yet know, and here is what we are measuring to find out" without discomfort. Someone who has merely studied the topic can recite the production-evaluation distinction and will still, on a Tuesday afternoon under deadline, open the draft first.

12. What each protagonist decided

Rhea submitted her plan on 19 March. She cut the APM cohort from nine to six, not because juniors were less valuable but because H at nine was 88 hours and at six was 132, and the curve in Figure 2 is steep in exactly that range. She costed the coaching explicitly — 792 senior hours, about ₹21 lakh of loaded senior time — and put it in the plan as a line item rather than leaving it as goodwill, on the argument that an invisible cost is the first cost cut. She restarted the prediction log on the decoupled design from Example three, and she committed to publishing the overconfidence gap quarterly, which is the one number that reveals whether the machine is running.

Kunal made the opposite-looking decision for a consistent reason. He gave Nikhil and Divya the Al Tayseer discovery, but he changed the structure: every requirement went first to a written pre-commitment from the APM, then to Shirin in Singapore for objection, then to the customer. Shirin's objection became the feedback loop rather than the obstacle, and her role was made explicit and credited. Kunal's reasoning was that his environment's problem was q, not H, and that Shirin's nineteen-year counterpart at Al Tayseer was not a reason to keep juniors away from the work but the best source of fast correction he had.

Discussion questions.

1. Rhea reduced her cohort in order to raise attention per junior; Kunal expanded his juniors' scope in order to raise feedback quality. Under what conditions is each the right move, and what would you need to observe in an organisation to tell which situation you are in?

2. The Substrate school holds that you cannot evaluate what you have never produced. Design an experiment a single company could actually run over eighteen months that would distinguish this claim from the Compression school's. What would it cost, and what would make the result uninterpretable?

3. If the Pipeline-economics school is right that no individual firm will fund general training, what institution should — business schools, professional bodies, the firms collectively — and what would that institution have to produce for a hiring manager to trust its output more than three years at a competitor?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does. The entry path is what is being rethought here, so the shape of the destination role determines which of the four schools is even coherent. Read it to fix the target before arguing about the route.
